entry.title: Ironwood · Day 5: The Chalk Cross the Rain Took Before Anyone Could Read It
entry.content:
Sunday 8 July 2046, morning

Vote YES on the Linden Rise drainage levy: clean water, clean lanes, sound pipes for every street.Printed leaflet, Linden Rise ward referendum

Amara Nwosu was at the culvert by twenty to ten on Sunday, on the dry side of the drain lake, her boots where the water stopped and the meter buckled into her satchel. The sky over Linden Rise was flat grey. Every so often a lorry went over the ring road on its pillars with a sound like a wardrobe dragged across a floor upstairs. The lake still lay over the path by the grate, and more of the reeds at the culvert mouth had gone black at the root than on Thursday.

She hadn't gone near. Isabel's text had said not to, so she had stood here twenty minutes doing what it said, with the signal behind her teeth like a drill in somebody else's flat. It was sharper than Thursday. When she turned her head toward the grate it sharpened again, and when she turned away it eased, as if it had a direction and the direction was her.

The plan was one reading she could trust, with Isabel watching, and Isabel saying it was right. What she'd turned over the whole way down the crescent was the other thing: that Isabel would ask her something too late for any excuse to hold.

Isabel came down the path from the Centre at five to, off the train at Breen's Crossing and the bus out, in the thin black jacket, her right hand flat inside the front of it against her ribs. The gauze showed at the cuff, browner than Thursday, and the first two fingers were strapped together.

"You waited," Isabel said.

"You said to."

Isabel stood and listened with her head on one side. "It's louder."

"It was louder Thursday. Today it's sharper." Amara heard herself. "Is that a dumb thing to say?"

"No. Sharper's right." Isabel looked at the grate, not at her. "Okay. Two things, before anything. Nerves first. If it's grown nerves you take them before you go near the rest, or it feels you and runs. And you never walk up on one alone."

"I'm not alone. You're here."

"That's why I'm here." Isabel's left thumb went along the strapped fingers through the jacket. "Natalie told me both of those my first night with a staff. She never said why about the second one. I found out yesterday. There was one under a block near mine, in the cellar, and I went down on my own with my back to the door, and it came up behind me. Between me and the stairs." She stopped there. "It waited till I was facing the wrong way."

"Did it get you?"

"It went round me." She took the hand out long enough to show it, and put it back. "So. One of you looks at it. One of you looks behind. Whoever's looking behind says when it moves."

Amara had it whole the first time, like the last line of a proof. "One looks at it, one looks behind, the one behind says when it moves. And the one in front says before she moves."

"Yeah." Isabel looked at her properly then. "Thursday your feet knew that bank. You went along it like you'd stood at one before. Have you? Not this one. Any."

There it was, early, and still too late for an excuse. "I come down here loads. It's on the way back from school." Amara took the meter out. "And I've read everything. There's a girl in Corrigan on the forums who drew diagrams of banks."

"That's not what I asked."

"I know the bank because I've walked the bank." She held up the box. "Can I do it now? I'll tell you before every step."

Isabel's mouth flattened, and she nodded at the water.

Amara called her staff. It came green into her hand, smelling of sap, and the copper ran warm down both forearms like the inside of a two-pence piece held to a lamp, and her shape came over her. From up here the lake looked smaller. Isabel came to her chin. Nothing anywhere was in a hurry, not the lorries, not the water, not her.

Isabel didn't call hers yet. She stood a step behind on the path, half turned, so she had the grate and the path back to the bus stop both.

The needle rested where it always rested now, a hair above zero, off the bent pin. Amara had done the sums last night: take that off whatever it read, and what was left was true. "That's rest," she said. "Two steps. To the edge."

"Go."

Two steps. The needle lifted to the first mark.

"One more. In to my ankle. Then I hold it out and I don't move my feet."

"Okay."

The water came cold over her boot. The needle climbed to the second mark, and the third, and the signal thinned to a bright wire, and behind the grate the thing turned. Not toward Isabel. Toward her.

"It's turned," she said. "It's facing me."

"Then come back. Say it and come back."

The needle was at the last mark and still climbing. If it stopped short of the stop, she could subtract and know. If it hit the stop, it was the pin or it was the thing, and she'd never know which, and Thursday's reading had ended the same way, rattling in the bottom of the box. One more second, and she'd have a number to show, and Isabel would have to say it was right.

"I'm holding it out," she said. "Feet still." She put the box toward the bars at the full length of her arm.

The needle hit the stop and stayed.

A thread came out between the bars, pale and finger-thin, fast along the top of the water, and laid itself across the back of her right hand where it held the box. She knew what it was before it hurt. Then it hurt.

Isabel called hers on the move. The pale staff was in the water beside Amara's before Amara heard her step off the path. She had it in her left hand only, and she laid it across the thread where it lay on Amara's skin and leaned, and the thread turned grey and came off into the lake in flakes. Under the road the rest of it drew back, the signal thinning, then far.

Isabel's shape was gone off her at once. She was down on one knee in the shallows with nothing in her hands, her right hand pressed into her stomach, the lake over the gauze.

Amara backed on to the path and let her own shape go. The scald ran from her first knuckle to the wrist bone, as wide as a shoelace, copper-coloured, wet down the middle. She shook the box. The needle came off the stop and fell back to a hair above zero.

So it had gone to the end, and the end was only the end. She had a new scald for a reading that said nothing.

Isabel got up out of the water soaked to the thigh and looked at Amara's hand.

"It went for you," she said. "I was right there, and it went past me for you. Again." She was breathing hard. "Amara. Have you done a cut before? On your own. Yes or no."

"I said before I moved. Every time. You heard me."

"You did."

That was nearly it. Amara waited for the rest, for that was right, and Isabel was already past it.

"That's not what I'm asking."

"I never got near it. You said nerves first, and I wasn't close enough to touch one."

"Your mum's Second Growth," Isabel said. "Hyejin told somebody you had this at the Tangle yesterday."

So Hyejin had said it after all, to someone, who'd said it to Isabel. All Amara had left was her face, and she kept it still.

"Mum runs consultations. She plans the rooms." She put the box in the satchel. "It's for physics. Interference."

Isabel looked at her, then up at the ring road, where a bus was coming round the long bend toward the Centre. Amara watched her work something out, and watched it come out against her.

"That's the twelve-ten," Isabel said. "I'll get that one. Next time tell me what you already know, first. Then I'll know what I'm teaching."

"Okay."

They went up the path together. Out of the shape Amara was shorter than Isabel again, level with her ear, the school jacket loose at the shoulders.

"You were taller than me down there," Isabel said.

"I'm still growing," Amara said. "Mum bought the jacket big for it."

Isabel looked at her sideways, and then at the bus.

"I'll walk you to the stop," Amara said, and Isabel let her.

Natalie came into Kell's Lane from the Linnet Lane end a little after twelve, under a sky gone low, with the river smell coming ahead of the rain. Iz would be at Linden Rise by now, on the far side of the ring road, on a bank beside the Second Growth woman's girl. Mrs Vella was out on her back step with the thermos before Natalie was halfway down.

"You're the other one," Mrs Vella said. "From Friday."

"Natalie."

"She's not here. Went off for the train this morning with a bag."

"I know."

The seam had nearly gone. On Friday it had run crooked a metre back from the downpipe; today the mortar there had closed and dried, and if Natalie hadn't watched it close she'd have walked past. What was left lay further along the foot of the wall, fainter, and it had crept since Friday a hand at a time toward the fire stair. The itch was hardly there. She stood still on the cobbles and waited for it, and it came and went like a radio between stations.

She only wanted to know how far it had got, so Iz wouldn't come back to it blind with a hand that didn't close. If she called her staff and opened it, she'd be on her knees in this lane holding it, and it would be hers again, and Iz would have it from Mrs Vella by teatime. It was a thing to find the end of, and leave.

She got down by the wall.

Her right palm was under fresh gauze, the Salter's Lane scald torn open in the middle on the Tangle's gate yesterday, and through the gauze the stones felt of nothing. She peeled the dressing back off the heel of her hand and laid the palm flat on the mortar.

The knit was there, a warmth under the cold a finger wide. She followed it a hand's width at a time. It didn't run straight. It wandered up into the second course of bricks and down again, and twice it dropped out and she had to go back to where she'd last had it and come at it again. The second time the soft middle of the scald opened on the grit.

"Who's coming to see to it?" Mrs Vella said.

"It's slow," Natalie said. "It won't do much this week."

"That's not who."

"Someone who knows the lane."

"Her, you mean. With the hand." Mrs Vella poured a mug and kept it. "When?"

"When the hand's better."

"And till then I keep the little ones off three drains and a downpipe, on the say of two girls who won't tell me what's in them." She set the mug on the step beside her. "The council's been saying someone'll come since Tuesday. I'd like it from a person, once."

Natalie lifted her hand. It had left copper-brown in the grit. She put it back. "Keep them off the drains. Both lanes. That's the most use anybody can be to you this week."

"You're as bad as she is."

A metre short of the fire stair the knit dropped out under her palm and didn't come back. She waited. She moved her hand right along the brick, and left, and down to the join with the cobbles, and there was the cold of the stone and the grit in the wet of the scald and nothing else. It might have gone on under the stair, or into the wall, or down. With the palm like this she couldn't tell which, and to find out she'd have to call the staff.

She sat back on her heels. The gauze wouldn't go back on; it slid on the wet and folded over on itself, and she left it hanging off her wrist.

On the step, among the things the little ones from number nine had left, there was a tin of coloured chalks. "Can I borrow one of those?"

Mrs Vella pushed the tin along with her foot. Natalie took the white in her left hand, which didn't know how, and drew a cross on the bottom brick by the fire stair, low, where the knit had dropped out. One arm came out longer than the other. It was the mark she put on a wall on her round when a thing wanted coming back to. Iz had walked five years behind her watching her put it there.

"What's that when it's at home?"

"Where it got to."

"I'll tell her you were here, then," Mrs Vella said, "since you won't." She held out the mug.

Natalie took it left-handed and drank it standing, too hot and too sweet, the right hand open at her side. If she went home for a week, there'd be a good many crosses for Iz to read.

She gave the mug back and went up the lane ahead of the rain, the chalk still in her left hand.

The rain had come in off the river by the time Isabel got off the train, and at half past four Kell's Lane was running with it, the cobbles shining, her jeans wet from the lake to the thigh and wet again now from the knee. Her right hand had nothing left in it. The strapped fingers wouldn't bend, and somewhere on the train the rest of the hand had stopped being any use. She'd promised Mrs Vella the cellar over a cup of tea and she'd come to keep it, and she'd decided on the walk up not to go near the wall. Natalie had said leave it.

Mrs Vella had her coat on and came out under the little porch over her step before Isabel reached the downpipe.

"Your Natalie was here," she said. "Dinnertime. Half an hour on her knees with her hand on the wall. She's left you something."

At the foot of the fire stair, on the bottom brick, was a chalk cross, white and crooked, one arm longer than the other. The rain had got to it already.

Isabel knew that cross. Five years of dawn rounds behind Natalie, and that was what went on a wall when Natalie meant to come back: the gutter at Chandler's Row, the chapel yard before a frost. Natalie's mark, for Natalie. Leave Kell's Lane till I can come with you, and then she'd come without her, the one morning Isabel was a train-line off.

Or it was for Isabel, like a note left on the fridge. She couldn't tell from here, and she wasn't going to ask Mrs Vella what Natalie's face had been doing while she drew it. If it marked something, she could at least hear what.

She crouched by the cross with her bad hand against her chest, shut her eyes, and listened for the static.

Fainter than any day this week. The rain was in everything, on the cobbles, in the downpipe, off the fire stair in a long thin stream, and the static was under all of it if it was there at all, one word in ten on a bad line. She got down on her knees on the wet stones and put her ear nearer the bottom course of bricks. There: a breath of it, toward the stair. Then nothing. She shuffled a hand's width along and listened again, and the downpipe gurgled over it, and when the downpipe stopped there was only rain.

With her staff the line would have come up under her like a road under headlights. But at the culvert this morning she'd had the wood in her left hand and the right pressed into her stomach, and she'd held it seconds. She stayed on her knees.

When she opened her eyes the cross had run. The long arm was a white streak down the brick and the short one a smudge. Whatever place Natalie had meant, it wasn't on the wall any more.

"You'll catch your death," Mrs Vella said. "In. Now."

The kitchen was hot, the radio low, a plate of biscuits nobody had asked for. Isabel sat at the table with her jacket dripping on the lino and the mug in her left hand.

"The cellar," Mrs Vella said. "You promised."

She'd tried ways of saying it on the train and none had come out right, so she said it plain. "There's something in the drain. Not rats. Not the pipe. It sits where the new pipe joins the old one. It was probably there in ninety-eight. It's why the cellar smells."

"Then that's the council's."

"The council can't see it. They'll send a man with a camera and he'll see a stain."

"And you can see it."

"Yeah."

Mrs Vella looked at the gauze on the table. "The Grech boy."

"I don't know," Isabel said. "Maybe." She put the mug down. "It's not where it was, though. So it's every drain on both lanes, not just the downpipe. Till I say."

Mrs Vella sat with both hands round her own mug, and Isabel watched her go back through forty years of the lane and find the year, and the boy, and believe it.

"Till you say," Mrs Vella said. "Then you'll say. Every night, six o'clock, at that door, where it's got to. I'm not having it off a chalk mark."

"I could text you."

"I don't text. At that door, or I'm on to the council again in the morning, and the paper after, and they can have the lane up like ninety-eight."

Men with spades in the lane, and the thing under it feeling every one of them. Six, every night. Isabel saw it go into the week before she could stop it: six here, and Linden Rise whenever Amara texted, cut short to make the train back, and five on Tuesday at Salter's Lane, and whatever was left over for Weir Street, which last night had been nothing, because she'd said no to it, and now every evening there'd be this door first.

"Six," she said.

She drank the tea, which was stewed, and ate a biscuit because Mrs Vella was watching her not eat one. Ten past five by Mrs Vella's clock. In rain like this the tram stop grate went under first, and Natalie would be out to it by now, and home after along the towpath, because it was the short way. The towpath went under the bridge.

Isabel put her jacket on wet and went out into it.

The long grate under the tram stop was under a hand of brown water by six, and Natalie did it from the kerb side, kneeling, left-handed, as she had yesterday. In the shelter, with the rain loud on the roof, she took her mother's letter out and looked at the fourteenth on the first page and the fourth on the second, and put it back against the lining before the wet could get to it.

She went back along the Tangle's wall. The flyers had gone to pulp on the poles, the drawn vines running down them in green streaks, and the stall's shutter was down. Past the gate the wall ended and the towpath began, and the canal was over its lip, a skin of water across the gravel with the current pulling at it.

She could have gone up Lockyer Street and round. But her boots had been wet since Friday, and the towpath was the short way home, and she meant to stay on the gravel the whole length of it.

Her phone went in her coat as she came level with the bridge. Mum, the screen said: her mother, Ruth, in Port Ellery.

"Natty. You got my letter."

"I got it, Mum."

"You've not written back."

"I was going to."

"Don't write. Say. Are you coming?"

The patch was under the bridge where it always was, and it pulled. The water was up to the lower rim of the hatch, brown and moving. Natalie kept her eyes on the far bank.

"I've a round, Mum. Twice a week. Somebody has to walk it."

"Then get somebody. You've had thirty years to find somebody." Ruth's voice was louder than Natalie remembered, and higher. "I've put you down. It's written. You can't say no to a thing once it's written."

"I haven't said no."

"You haven't said anything."

The pull came low and steady, a floor tipping toward the water. She fixed on the council notice cable-tied to the railing across the canal, warning against the towpath after heavy rain, and answered her mother, and somewhere between one line and the next she was on the grass at the top of the bank, and then going down it sideways with her weight on her heels and the phone at her ear. The water came over her boots and up through the stiff trouser leg to her knees. Her left hand was flat on the iron plate of the hatch.

"Nat."

Iz was on the towpath above her, soaked through, her jacket stuck to her, the bad hand held against her chest. She had come from the lock end, where anyone would come from who knew which grate flooded first and how long Natalie took over it. She was looking at the hand on the hatch.

Natalie took her hand off the iron. That was all she could do about it now.

"Who's that?" Ruth said. "Is someone with you?"

"A friend, Mum."

Iz's face went still under the bridge lamp. Natalie heard Elspeth in it half a second after Iz did.

"Natty, I want you there for it. I want you to see me do it properly."

"I'll ring you back. Tonight."

"You won't."

"I will." She ended the call with her right thumb, and the scald across her palm caught on the edge of the case and opened again.

"Get out of there," Iz said.

The bank was steeper going up. Iz came down two steps and held out her left hand, and Natalie took it with hers, and Iz pulled, and her foot slid on the wet grass and her knee went into the mud, and she was still holding on. Natalie came up past her on to the gravel. Water ran out of her boots.

"That was your mum," Iz said, still on her knee.

"Yes."

"And the letter."

"It's from home."

"What does it say? Is that August? Is that what Tuesday was?"

"Tuesday's Salter's Lane."

In her coat the phone went again. Natalie put her hand flat over the pocket and kept it there, the thing buzzing against the open scald, until it stopped.

"You're not going to get that."

"I said tonight."

"Tonight for what?" Iz got up. "And who walks your round, if you go wherever she wants you? Because it's me, isn't it, it was always going to be me, you just haven't asked." She stopped. "A friend."

"I wasn't going to explain you to her down a phone, on a towpath."

It answered the last thing Iz had said and nothing before it, and Natalie watched her know it.

"Your cross on Kell's Lane ran," Iz said. "I couldn't hear a thing, and then it was off the brick before I'd worked out what it was for. You told me to leave that lane till you could come with me, and then you went without me." She was breathing hard. "So I'll find it, and I'll go down after it, and you'll be under the stair, and my name still won't go in the book."

Natalie looked at her. Iz's shoulders were up round her ears, the way they were at four in the morning on the round when she'd decided she was cold and wasn't going to say so. There was mud to her knee, and the gauze on her hand was grey with rain. Elspeth was still holding the Hundred and Fourth. It was the one true thing Natalie could put in Iz's hands tonight.

"Have you still got the jar?" Natalie asked.

Iz stared at her. "In the drawer. Clean."

"Keep it there."

They went along the towpath toward the lock with the water over their boots. At the bridge Iz stepped round behind her to the canal side, so that she was between Natalie and the water, and walked there all the way to the lock.

entry.title: Ironwood · Day 4: The Stall Woman Gave a Girl a Tomato and Asked Nothing
entry.content:
Saturday 7 July 2046, morning

Keep off the drains on Linnet Lane. Ask before you go down.Handwritten note pinned inside the lobby of Kell's Lane block, 4 Kell's Lane

Amara Nwosu came off the tram at the top of Lockyer Street a step behind Mum, with the satchel strap across her chest and the meter inside it, and the dressing on her wrist under two sleeves. It was Saturday. Mum worked for Second Growth, which wanted to build its hall on the edge of the Tangle, and she was walking the site once more before Tuesday's consultation. She had brought Amara rather than leave her at home on Rowan Crescent with an arm she didn't trust. Her lanyard was on, though nobody was paying her today.

Lockyer Street ran down toward the canal between old warehouses with flats in them. Halfway down, a white van was parked half on the kerb with the Second Growth leaf on its side. As Amara passed it the satchel swung hard against her hip, out and back, twice, though she hadn't changed her step. She put her hand flat on the flap and kept walking. The signal behind her teeth stayed quiet the whole length of the van, and quiet after it, and she looked back at the leaf on its side door until Mum said her name.

At the bottom the wall began, long and brick, with trees standing up over it much too big for a park. There was a flyer on every pole, SAVE THE TANGLE over a drawn vine. By the gate a stall had its shutter up and its trestles out, and in the window behind the tomatoes sat a council notice about the hall, curling at the corners. A woman with greying hair tied back in green garden twine was weighing tomatoes for an old man in a cap. Amara had bought tomatoes from this stall last summer, a whole bag, while Mum walked the site with her plans. She'd been a different person last summer. She hadn't owned a box.

"Can I walk to the end and back?" she asked. "You'd see me the whole way. It's straight."

"To the gate," Mum said. "Where I can see you without turning round."

"The gate's right there."

"Then it won't take you long."

Mum went up to the stall with her meeting face on, the friendly one. "Morning. You'll be Hyejin Park. Your name's on every pole from the tram."

Amara stopped with her hand on the satchel buckle.

Hyejin Park. Three messages, the night Amara had posted about the culvert: what it costs, how girls die, that nobody is coming. She'd read each one twice under the duvet with the brightness all the way down, and answered none of them, because answering would have made them true. She'd pictured someone old and certain, in a dark room somewhere. Not dirt in the creases of her hands. Not weighing tomatoes for a man in a cap.

She looked at the trestle, and the scales, and the kerb, and anywhere that wasn't Hyejin's face. Hyejin didn't know her face. There was no reason she would. Amara made herself breathe through her nose, slowly, the way she did before an exam.

"And you're the hall," Hyejin said.

"I'm Chioma Nwosu. I'm running Tuesday evening. I wanted to see it in daylight before I stand up in front of people who love it."

"Then tell me in daylight. Why here? There's the old gasworks. There's half of Corrigan standing empty."

Amara went along to the gate, not fast. It was iron, painted green a long time ago, and the trees inside came right up to it. She turned her back to the stall, so her body was between the box and Mum, and took the meter out and held it low against her side.

The needle sat where it always sat now, a hair above zero, where the pin had bent. She tipped the box toward the gate. The needle lifted past the first felt-tip mark, and on, slowly, to the second, and stayed there. She turned it toward the wall. It dropped a little. Back to the gate, and up to the second again, steady, not jumping as it had at the culvert.

Two marks, less whatever the bent pin added. She'd only ever measured that at rest. Out here it could be anything, and she wanted it to be real so badly that she didn't trust herself to read it.

"The canal water," Mum was saying behind her, "and where the grid comes in. You'll have all of it Tuesday, with the maps."

"I've seen the maps."

"Then you've seen why."

"I've seen a car park drawn over my beds."

Amara knew this one. Mum did it at parents' evenings and at Aunty Ngozi's, when the conversation went somewhere she didn't want it: she agreed with the part that didn't matter, and moved on to the bit she'd chosen before she arrived. She'd say Tuesday again in a minute. She'd say it so kindly that Hyejin would have to be rude to push past it.

"I'd rather say it once, properly, with everyone there," Mum said. "If I give you half of it at a stall, half is what goes round."

"Have you been in? Past the gate? Have you put your hand in those beds?"

"I have. It's remarkable. I'm not going to stand up Tuesday and pretend it isn't."

There. Tuesday, and kind with it. Hyejin had a bunch of string in one hand and she pulled it tight round nothing.

"We'll have three hundred names on Tuesday," she said. "Three hundred, from this street and the next two."

"Good. Bring them all. I mean that."

Amara glanced back. Mum had her notebook open on the end of the trestle, and she was writing 300 with a line under it. Hyejin had meant it as a threat, and Mum was writing it down as a number of chairs. Amara felt sorry for Hyejin for a second, and then remembered who Hyejin was, and didn't know what to feel.

She moved a step closer to the bars. The needle went no higher. One more, from the corner where the wall met the gatepost, and she'd know if it was the gate or what was behind it.

"What's she reading?"

Hyejin's voice had changed direction. Amara's head came round before she could stop it. Hyejin was looking past Mum's shoulder straight at her, at the box, and then lower, at her left wrist, where the sleeve had ridden up off the edge of the white dressing.

Amara's whole skin went hot. She couldn't get the box down. Her hand had forgotten how.

"Oh, it's a thing she built," Mum said. "She points it at everything. We're out at Linden Rise, and she's had it at every drain on the estate."

Mum. Linden Rise, out loud, across the tomatoes, to the one person in the Bay who had written to a girl at Linden Rise and got nothing back. Amara watched Hyejin put it together: the estate, the box, the wrist. The girl who hadn't answered. If she said it now, she'd say it to Mum. If she didn't say it now, she could say it to Isabel, or say it on Tuesday in front of three hundred names, any time she liked, for as long as she liked.

Amara put the box back in the satchel and got the buckle done on the second go. "It's for physics," she said. Her voice came out too high. "Interference. It's not very good yet."

"Mm," Hyejin said.

She picked a tomato off the top of the pile, the reddest one, and held it out over the trestle. Amara had to come and take it. She didn't see how not to. It was warm, though the morning wasn't.

"On the house," Hyejin said, to Amara and not to Mum. "Grown just there. You'll be at the back on Tuesday, I expect."

Mum paid for a kilo and said thank you, and took Amara's elbow, the good one, and they walked back up Lockyer Street past the van.

Amara held the tomato in her right hand the whole way to the tram. Grown just there, behind the gate the needle had climbed for. Hyejin hadn't said a word about the messages. She'd said you'll be at the back, as if she'd already put Amara somewhere, and she'd given her a thing from inside the wall to carry home in front of her mother. It might have been kind. It might have been the opposite of kind. Amara turned it over on the tram, and turned it back, and couldn't decide whether she was meant to eat it or keep it, or what it said about her either way.

Isabel came back to Kell's Lane at midday with the pesto jar in her jacket and her right hand in her pocket, and found Mrs Vella already at the downpipe in her coat, holding a key on a loop of string.

The static was fainter than yesterday. Isabel had to stand still at the drain grate at the foot of the downpipe with her eyes shut before she found it at all, a weak signal behind her ear that cut out for five seconds at a time. Along the foot of the wall the seam she'd opened and lost had closed over again, crooked, the mortar knitting back in a line that wandered off from where her staff had run. Yesterday it would have taken an hour to open. Today she wasn't sure she could find enough of it to start.

"That's the cellar," Mrs Vella said, and held the key up. "The block's. I've had it since the caretaker died in oh-three, and nobody's ever asked for it back."

"Can I borrow it?"

"You can tell me first whether the little ones from number nine are safe. I've rung the council three times now. The girl on the phone said someone would come and look at the drains. Nobody's come and looked at the drains, love, except you."

"They're safe if they keep off them."

"That's not safe, that's careful." Mrs Vella turned the key on its string. "In ninety-eight they had this lane up seven weeks. The old drain's brick, under Linnet Lane, from when the lanes were laid. They ran the new pipe from the downpipe under the block and joined it on to the brick one, under the cellar floor, and that joint never sat right. Every winter since, that cellar's smelled. The Grech boy at number four was poorly the whole of that year and nobody could say with what." She held the key out. "You come up and tell me what you find. Whatever it is."

"I'll tell you," Isabel said, and took it in her left hand.

The cellar door was round the side of the block under the fire stair, and the steps went down steep into a smell of wet brick. Mrs Vella stayed at the top with her hand on the rail.

At the bottom there was a bulb that didn't work, a row of meters, three bins and a pram with no wheels. Isabel stood on the concrete. Natalie was on Weir Street, ten minutes away. If Isabel went and got her, Natalie would come down these steps first, and it would be Natalie's root again, and Natalie's jar, and Isabel holding the torch. She called her staff.

The pale wood came into her hands and the copper ran down both forearms, and the shape settled over her.

Her right hand hadn't closed past halfway since yesterday morning. She'd meant to hold her phone in it for the torch. It wouldn't hold the phone and the staff both, and the phone slid down her fingers on to the concrete, so she left it there face up, throwing a white circle on the ceiling, and worked by what came back off the walls.

The static came up through the floor, or seemed to. The crooked knit was in the floor too, a line where the damp wouldn't sit, and she followed that with the staff end, a hand's width at a time. It ran across the slab from the side nearest the lane toward the back wall, the Linnet Lane side, wandering left of where any pipe ought to go. Twice the static dropped out altogether and she stood in the dark with the staff on the concrete and waited for it, and twice it came back fainter, from nowhere she could point to.

By the back wall there was an inspection cover set into the floor, cast iron, the size of a tea tray. The knit ran straight to it.

She put the staff in the crook of her left arm and got her fingers under the edge of the lid. It was heavy. She got it up a hand's width with her left hand and the heel of her right, and looked under.

The brick drain ran across under the lid, and on the joint where the new pipe met it there was a dark stain on the brick, warm, the air over it moving a little. Nothing else. Whatever had sat there had gone.

Then the static came, loud, from behind her.

Not from the drain. From the lane side of the cellar, under the bins, the way she'd come in. Between her and the stairs.

She turned too fast. The lid came out of her hands and down into its frame and took the first two fingers of her right hand with it, iron on iron on knuckle. She heard herself make a noise. The static went up, and up, louder than it had been all week, so loud it wasn't behind her ear any more but in her teeth, and she was on one knee with her hand trapped and the staff sliding off her arm and she thought, very clearly, this is why. Never walk up on one alone. Natalie had said it the first night, and never said why, and here was why, under the bins, coming.

She got her fingers out. She got the staff up.

The static was already going. From loud to far, down and along under the side wall, and halfway it dropped out and didn't come back. Toward Linnet Lane, or back under Kell's Lane. It hadn't come at her. It had gone round her.

"Fuck," Isabel said, to the cellar. "Fuck, fuck."

Her hand was hot under the gauze and getting wet. She held it against her stomach and breathed through her teeth until she could think past it, and what she thought was worse. It had sat under this block for two days with nobody near it, and it had waited for her to come down the stairs before it moved. A root with no nerves didn't do that. She had taken every nerve it had on Tuesday night. It had felt her crossing a cellar floor in the dark, and let her get all the way to the far wall with her back to it.

She stood with the staff until she was sure there was nothing to hear. She let the shape go, and the cold came in through her jacket. Picking her phone up off the floor took her three goes with the left hand, and she swore at it every time. When she went up the steps she held the rail with her elbow.

"Well?" Mrs Vella said.

"I don't know where it is," Isabel said. "The smell. It was here and it isn't. Keep them off the drains on Linnet Lane as well."

Mrs Vella looked at her for a while, and at the gauze, which had gone brown at the knuckles. "That's my side."

"I know."

"Then you'd better come in and have a cup of tea and tell me what that means," Mrs Vella said, and held out her hand for the key, and waited.

The rain came back to the old core in the middle of the afternoon, and by four Natalie was out in it, going down to look at the long grate under the tram stop. The towpath was the quick way, and she didn't take the towpath with the water up. She went round by Lockyer Street instead, along the Tangle's wall, which she hadn't walked the length of since spring, and came round the corner of the stall before she'd thought about whose stall it was.

Hyejin Park had it half packed in the wet, crates of tomatoes stacked under a tarp, the council notice in the window gone soft and dark at its corners. She was folding a trestle. She looked up, and for a second neither of them did anything at all.

"Nat."

"I'm going to the tram stop," Natalie said.

"I can see where you're going." Hyejin got the trestle flat and leaned it on the wall. "Your Second Growth woman walked the site this morning. She brought her girl. The girl had a box."

"She's not mine."

"The girl's from Linden Rise." Hyejin pushed wet hair off her face with her wrist. "I wrote to a girl at Linden Rise."

A box with a needle that went to the stop. Iz had told her all of it under the pole on Thursday night. If Natalie walked on now, Hyejin would know that she knew. She stopped.

"I'll take some beans, if you've any left."

Hyejin found half a bag under the tarp and didn't weigh it. She held it out, and when Natalie reached for it she didn't let go straight away.

"Come in and see the beds. Five minutes. The rain's nothing under the trees."

The canal was up. Natalie could hear it past the end of the wall, louder than this morning, and she knew without looking how high it would be against the stone at the bridge, and where the hatch was, under it, and that it would be pulling. Hyejin had come round the end of the stall to the gate. From there she could see along the towpath to the bridge as well as Natalie could.

Natalie kept her eyes on Hyejin.

"Twenty-one years I've walked past this gate," she said. "I'm not starting today."

"Then don't start. Just come in the once." Hyejin had the twine come loose at the back of her hair. "They'll pave it inside a year, Nat. Then you won't have to walk past it ever again. You'll have that."

"Don't."

The pull came stronger, low in her, like the slope of a floor that tipped toward the water. Her head wanted to turn. To give her hand something to do instead, Natalie put her right palm on the gate. She had a scald across the base of that palm, over the callus, from the grate in Salter's Lane, wet and soft in the middle. The bar was cold and wet. She held it, and kept her face on Hyejin's, and pressed, and the soft middle of the scald tore open against the iron. It hurt cleanly. It was a thing to hold on to that wasn't the bridge, and she kept holding.

Hyejin put her hand on the gate too, a bar along.

"I was on that bridge," she said.

The rain ran off the end of the stall. Hyejin's hands had gone still on the bar, gardener's hands, dirt in the creases.

"I know where you were," Natalie said. "I'm going to the tram stop."

She took her hand off the gate. There was copper-brown on the green paint where her palm had been, a smear of it, and the rain started on it at once. Hyejin looked at the bar and then at the hand.

"What's that?"

"Salter's Lane. The frost had it in the iron."

"You want that wrapped."

"I've stuff at home." Natalie put the hand in her coat pocket and her fingers found the letter there, and she moved them off it. "What do I owe you?"

"Nothing."

Natalie got her phone out left-handed and held it to the reader on the end of the trestle anyway, until it chirped. Hyejin's pocket buzzed. She didn't take it out. She turned her back and went on pulling the tarp over the crates, tucking the corners under, one and then the next, harder than the job needed.

When Natalie got to the tram stop, the grate was under four fingers of brown water. She did it from the kerb side, kneeling, with the staff in her left hand, and her right in her pocket, bleeding into the lining.

Isabel came up the stairs on Weir Street a little after eight with the rain still on her jacket. Natalie had the door open before she knocked, and the kettle was already going.

Natalie's boots stood on newspaper by the heater, toes to it, and the narrow strip of amber from the baseboard runner lay across the floorboards between them. Her right hand had new gauze on it, round the palm and between the thumb and finger.

"What happened?"

"Gate," Natalie said.

"What gate?"

"The Tangle's."

Isabel looked at her. "You went in the Tangle?"

"No." Natalie filled two mugs left-handed and slopped one. "Sit down. You've been at the lane."

Isabel didn't sit. She gave it to her in order, because she'd been putting it in order all the way over, on the tram, so it would come out without her voice doing anything: the key, the cellar, the cover, the stain. Then the static, behind her, by the door.

"It waited," she said. "Two days on its own under there and it waited till I was across the floor. Then it went round me."

Natalie went still, as she did over a grate before she said get back. "Which way?"

"I don't know. I lost it." She held up her hand, the gauze brown at the knuckles. "Lid came down on this."

"You went down there on your own."

"Mrs Vella was at the top of the stairs."

"Leave Kell's Lane, then," Natalie said. "Till I can come with you."

Four days she'd been fighting for that lane. Isabel looked at the stain on her gauze and thought about the static in her teeth, and found she didn't have it in her tonight to fight for it.

"Okay," she said, and hated how easy it came.

"Hyejin says the Second Growth woman's girl had a box at the Tangle this morning."

"Amara?" Isabel put the mug down. "Her mum's Second Growth? She never said." Of course she never said. Amara said three things and knew forty. "I'm at Linden Rise tomorrow, ten, at the culvert. She wants me to watch her hold the box to the grate."

"Good."

Natalie sat down on the arm of the sofa with her mug, under the tall glass, the radio towers blinking red on the ridge behind her in the rain. "Salter's Lane," she said. "If the thaw comes Tuesday, it's five in the morning. It's yours. I won't be there."

"Where will you be?"

"Here. In bed, if I've any sense."

"So I get your grate, on my own, with a hand that doesn't close, and you get my lane."

"The lane's got a root that can feel you coming. Salter's Lane is a grate you've watched me do fifty times."

"And the Friday after? The chapel yard? The tram stop?"

Natalie drank some of her tea.

The coat was on its hook by the door, olive and long. All week Natalie's hand had gone into the inside pocket of it and come out empty.

"What's in your pocket?"

"A letter."

"From who?"

"Home."

"Port Ellery." Isabel waited, and nothing else came. Five years, and Isabel knew the name of the town and that Natalie didn't go back to it, and that was all. "Is that Tuesday? Nobody plans a grate four days out, Nat. You don't. You go when it's thawed."

"Tuesday's Salter's Lane. If it thaws."

"You can't tell me, or you won't?"

It came out too loud for the flat. Natalie didn't answer that either, and Isabel heard herself go on, and couldn't stop. "My name's never gone in the book. Not once, in five years. Every jar's gone up that step in your hand. And now I get your round, with your letter in your coat, and I'm supposed to take that as a present."

Natalie put her mug down on the floor by her foot. She got up and came over and reached for Isabel's right hand, the bad one, to look at it.

Isabel pulled it back against her chest. "Don't."

Natalie stood with her own bandaged hand still half out, and then let it drop.

The rain went sideways across the glass. Natalie took Isabel's mug, which was still full, and put it on the bench beside the slopped one.

"Stay," she said. "It's pouring. You can get out to Linden Rise from here as easy as from yours."

And Isabel wanted to. That was the worst of it. She was working it out before she could stop herself: the 14 from Weir Street, the change at the station, the train up the line. It worked from here. It worked better from here. She could have the end of the sofa and the strip of amber on the floor, and Natalie making toast in the morning with the wrong hand, like Thursday. On Thursday she would have stayed without being asked.

But Natalie had asked after. After Salter's Lane, and after the letter that was none of Isabel's business. As if the one made up for the other.

"No," she said. "I'll go home."

She zipped her jacket, one-handed, which took two goes. "Five, Tuesday. Salter's Lane. From the top, not the bottom. Feel the iron first. I'll do it."

"Iz."

"I said I'll do it."

Natalie stood by the bench with her bandaged hand at her side. Isabel went past the coat on its hook to the door. Her sleeve brushed the hem of it, and the paper in the inside pocket made its small sound, and she opened the door and went down into the rain, and stood a minute at the bottom of the stairs, getting wet, before she made herself walk.

entry.title: Ironwood · Day 3: The Wall Closed Behind the Staff Before the Girl Was Called Off It
entry.content:
Friday 6 July 2046, morning

Tell me before you move. Don't leave it to the last minute.Scrawled on a fridge magnet note, Rowan Crescent

Natalie let herself out of her flat on Weir Street at a quarter to five and went down into the old core to walk her Friday round, into the first hard frost of the winter.

Everything had gone white in the night. The bluestone kerbs were furred with it, the cobbles in the lanes had a skin that took the print of her boots, and her breath stood in front of her face and stayed there. She had walked this round on Tuesdays and Fridays for twenty-nine years. Her feet took the corners before she did.

The first one was in the gutter at the foot of Chandler's Row, where it always came back: a grey stain on the stone the size of a dinner plate, warm enough underneath that the frost had gone off it in a ring. The itch sat faint at the back of her head. She called her staff, set the end of it on the stain and leaned, and the copper went out of her arms down the wood and into it, and it went to ash. She scuffed the ash into the crack between two stones and walked on. Four minutes.

The second was behind the bakery bins, under the downpipe, no bigger than a fist. Two minutes. A third, hardly anything, sat in the drain mouth on Bell Street. She did them the way Mum used to do the beans on the back step in Port Ellery: bent over, not looking up, moving along the row.

The grate in Salter's Lane was another thing. The itch was down in the iron. The cold had driven the blight into the bars the way it had stiffened the puddles, and when she set her staff on the grate and leaned, the copper went down the wood, stopped at the iron, and came back up her arms cold. She leaned again, harder, through her five minutes and then through five more. The frost went off the bars where the staff touched them and stayed white everywhere else.

At about the twelfth minute it bit. When she took her right hand off the staff there was a scald across the base of her palm, over the callus, a thumb wide and two thumbs long, copper-coloured, the skin gone wet and soft in the middle of the hard.

She looked at the grate. The root was still in the iron. It would sit there until a thaw loosened it, and then it would come up warm and want doing properly. She let the staff go and walked on with the hand open in the cold.

The round took her along the Tangle's wall next, the long brick side of it, with the trees standing up over the top much bigger than twenty-one years should have made them, white to the last twig. Every pole along the footpath had one of Hyejin's flyers on it, SAVE THE TANGLE over the hand-drawn vine, and the frost had got into the paper so the vines stood out stiff. The stall beside the gate had its shutter down. In its window the council's notice had curled at the corners and frozen that way. Natalie read it as she passed: PUBLIC CONSULTATION. PROPOSED SUBSTRATE HALL, EAST EDGE OF SITE. TUESDAY 10 JULY, 6.30 PM, CANAL COMMUNITY ROOMS. ALL WELCOME.

She walked a little nearer the gate than she generally did, near enough that the cold came off its bars onto her coat, and then she was past it, as she had been past it every Tuesday and Friday for twenty-one years, since there had first been a wall here to walk past.

At the corner where the lane came out on the towpath she stopped under the lamp and took Mum's letter out of her coat with her left hand.

Mum's writing had gone big and loose since the last letter, ten years back. Port Ellery at the top, underlined twice. A Tuesday in August, the fourteenth, and would Natty come home for it, and stay the week before, and be there. Natalie read the first page through. On the second, near the bottom, after a paragraph about the jetty being redone, Mum had written: So that's the 4th, love. Don't leave it to the last minute like you do.

She looked at the fourth for a while. She turned back to the first page and found the fourteenth where she had left it. She folded the letter along its old creases and put it back against the lining.

Beyond the lamp the canal was up to the lip of the towpath, skinned with ice along both edges and black and moving down the middle. The bridge stood over it white along its rail. The patch by the bridge was where it always was, and it pulled.

She meant to walk past it. She had walked past it on Tuesday.

She went down the bank on the frozen grass with her weight back on her heels. At the bottom the ice took one step and not the second, and her left boot went through into the canal. The water came over the top of the boot and up to the middle of her shin.

She stood in it. Under the bridge, set into the stonework above the waterline, the iron plate of the hatch had frost along its rim. Once the water had come to her hips in there, and she had waited with it climbing and listened and trembled. She'd gotten good at waiting. She went to leave, and found the water had left her foot numb. She scrabbled back up the bank with her hands, the scald on her palm opening on the frozen grass.

Her boot squelched for the rest of the round, and her trouser leg froze stiff from the knee down. She did the two grates past the lock, and the one in the chapel yard, and the long one under the tram stop that flooded first in any rain. At each of them she stood a moment longer than they should have needed. The chapel yard froze before anywhere else did. The tram stop one wanted doing from the kerb side, not the road. Salter's Lane wanted coming back to after a thaw, at five in the morning, by somebody who knew to feel for it in the iron.

At twenty to seven she turned north for Kell's Lane with the frost still on her shoulders, and no time to go home and change her boots.

Isabel was in Kell's Lane by half past six, on her knees on the frozen cobbles, feeling for the seam with her left fingertips before she called anything. The pesto jar was in her jacket, washed twice, the label and the glue scrubbed off, the lid screwed down. Both scalds were under chemist's gauze, the one from the culvert and yesterday's from this lane, crossing each other on the back of her right hand. Overnight they had stuck to themselves, and the hand didn't close all the way anymore.

The static was fainter than yesterday. She had to hold her breath to hear it, a bad line behind her ear that dropped out for whole seconds, and she followed it under the fire stair and along the foot of the wall toward the downpipe, where yesterday it had nearly shouted. The frost lay over the whole lane the same, seam or no seam.

She had the order worked out from the walk over. Natalie would come in at the end of the lane and stand there. Isabel would open the wall from the downpipe end, come round under the stair, find the root and kill it, and Natalie would watch her do it. If Natalie got down on her knees under that stair, Isabel would spend the morning holding a wall for her, and she'd be back on Garnet Street's step with a jar that wasn't hers.

Mrs Vella had come out on her back step in a coat over her dressing gown, with a thermos and two chipped mugs on the step beside her. Somewhere behind the wall the little ones from number nine were hunting for puddle ice to stamp on, giggles echoing through the alley.

"I've told them this end's mine this morning," Mrs Vella said. "Is it the drains? It's been a fridge down here since Tuesday night. I've rung the council twice and got a recording."

"Ask me at eight," Isabel said.

Natalie came into the lane at seven. There was frost on her shoulders and in her hair at the part. Her left trouser leg was dark from the knee down and stiff with it, white along the crease, and her boot left wet prints that went white behind her.

"Straight from the round," she said, before Isabel could ask where from.

So she'd walked her round and gone down to that bank again, by the bridge, and come here with it frozen up her leg, and that was the whole answer she was going to get. Isabel put it aside for the moment.

"I want the stair end too," she said. "I've been here since half past. I've got the line. You can watch from Mrs Vella's step."

"Stair end's mine. We said last night."

"You said Elspeth's holding the Hundred and Fourth. If you kill the root, it's yours. She'll know. She knows everything."

"She writes whoever brings the jar. That's you."

"That's not the same and you know it's not." Isabel tried the other way in. "And you've been up since four, and you've got a foot full of ice."

"And you've a hand that doesn't close."

"It closes."

"Close it, then."

Isabel closed it. She got it most of the way, to where her nails nearly touched her palm, and the gauze over her knuckles went dark from the inside, copper-brown, spreading out to the edges. She opened it again.

Natalie didn't say anything about the gauze. "Wall's yours," she said. "All four metres. I'll be under the stair, and I'll be watching you the whole way."

Mrs Vella unscrewed the thermos and poured. Natalie took a mug and drank it standing, far too hot, the steam going up past her face. Mrs Vella held out the other.

"In a minute," Isabel said.

Then she called her staff. The pale wood came into her hands and the copper ran warm down both forearms, and the shape settled over her, and she knelt in it a moment with the staff across her knees before she put it to the wall. Her right hand wouldn't grip. She held the staff in her left and pressed the heel of the right against it, flat, which put the weight in the wrong place and a strain on the scalds. Better than no weight at all.

She started at the downpipe and leaned. Her copper ran out along the staff into the knit where the wall met the cobbles, and it opened under her: a line along the mortar where the frost wouldn't lie, the width of a finger, warm. She moved the staff along it a hand's width at a time and held what was behind her.

Natalie was on her knees under the fire stair with her own staff in the dark of it, turned so she could see the length of the wall. "Tell me when you're at the stair," she said.

One metre. Two. The static came up loud now, interference on every channel, all of it at the wall. Her right hand slid on the wood and she put her shoulder behind it instead. Somewhere past three metres her shape thinned on her like breath going off glass, and behind her, at the downpipe, she felt the seam start to close: the first hand's width, then the next.

She could call out now. Natalie was right there. She'd come out from under the stair and lay her staff along the wall beside Isabel's, and it would be Natalie's wall as well as Natalie's root, and Isabel would carry the jar to Garnet Street for both of them.

So she didn't. She leaned harder and took the staff on another hand's width toward the stair. She was still a meter off, and the cut was closing behind her faster than she was opening in front.

"There," Natalie said, under the stair, and went in.

The root didn't wait for her. Isabel felt it go past under the wall, along the knit behind her staff, the way she'd let close, fast and low, and down. Under the stair the end Natalie had pinned went grey. At the downpipe the static dropped into the drain grate at its foot and settled there, under the block, steady.

The shape slipped off Isabel and she was on her knees on the cobbles with nothing in her hands.

Goddammit. She'd pushed so hard, and it wasn't enough, she still would have lost it no matter whether Natalie had waited or not. The root would have gone the same way, down the knit she couldn't hold, and under. She'd washed a jar twice for this. She'd planned it on the walk over, again and again. Stupid. Her eyes stung, and she let them.

Whether Natalie had gone in because she'd felt the root move or because she'd seen Isabel's shape going, Isabel couldn't tell from the lane.

The seam ran crooked and closed from the downpipe back along the wall for about a metre, and went into the drain at the foot of the downpipe. The root was under the building now, somewhere along the drain, out of reach of anything she could do from the lane.

Natalie came out from under the stair on her elbows. On the cobbles where she'd been lay a handful of grey ash, dry on the frost. Isabel's left hand went to her jacket, to the jar, and she gripped it tight.

"Well?" Mrs Vella said, from the step. "It's not eight, but you've both stopped."

"No," Isabel said. "It's not safe. Keep them off the downpipe and the drain at the bottom of it, as well as the stair. It's gone into the drain under the block."

"Under the block. That'll be the whole lane up, then, just like ninety-eight."

Mrs Vella poured the second mug and held it out again, and this time Isabel got up and took it in her left hand. The tea was stewed and much too sweet. She drank it standing beside Natalie, with the empty jar against her ribs.

Amara Nwosu had the meter open on the kitchen table on Rowan Crescent by half past seven: the lid off, the magnifying lamp brought down from her desk and clamped to the table's edge, the soldering iron heating in its stand. The sleeve of her hoodie was pulled down over her left wrist and held there with her thumb. Mum's car was still out the front. Mum would be down by quarter to.

The needle had come off its pin at the culvert, and the pin had bent where it hit the stop. She straightened it with the small pliers under the lamp, by eye, a little at a time, faster than she should have. Then the joint. It was the one she'd thought it was: dull and grainy, the wire lifting off the pad when she touched it with the tweezers. A cold joint. She put the iron to it and fed in fresh solder, and it ran bright and smooth and set.

The needle was harder. It wouldn't sit. It dropped off the pin twice into the bottom of the box, and the second time Mum's feet were on the stairs. Amara got it back with the tweezers and pressed it on, and it went, and it sat. When she let go, it didn't fall to zero. It rested a hair above it, just shy of the first felt-tip mark, because the pin hadn't come quite straight. She tapped the box. The needle stayed where it was. So the box held together now, and whatever it read, it would read that much high. Doing the pin again meant taking the needle off, and there wasn't time. She pulled her sleeve straight.

Mum came in with her work blazer on and the Second Growth lanyard already round her neck, and a sheaf of papers under one arm. The top one said CONSULTATION EVENING, CANAL COMMUNITY ROOMS, TUESDAY 10 JULY. She put them on the bench and switched the kettle on.

"The chicken was in the sink when I got home," Mum said. "The water had gone warm."

"I forgot. Sorry. I'll do dinner tonight."

"You said you'd do it now. At twelve." Mum turned round and leaned on the bench. "So you weren't here at three. Where were you?"

"Out testing this." Amara tipped the box toward her. "It picks up interference. I wanted to see what it did away from the house."

"Away from the house where?"

"Round the crescent. The Centre."

Mum looked at her the way she looked at the news when a councillor was talking, quite still. "Your jeans are in the machine with drain lake on them to the knee," she said. "You were down at the culvert. I'm not cross about the lake. I want to know who you were with."

That was the question, and it was too late for any of the three excuses. They'd all been for the start. "On my own," Amara said.

"On your own in that water."

"It's not deep. I had boots on."

The iron ticked in its stand. Mum came over and reached for the plug at the wall. "You'll have the house down with that thing on and you looking at me." Amara reached for it too, to do it herself, and her sleeve rode up off her wrist.

Mum took her hand and turned it over under the lamp.

The scald ran from the bone on the outside of her wrist a thumb's length up her forearm, about as wide as a shoelace, the colour of a new penny, still wet down the middle.

"What's this?"

"The iron. Wednesday night."

Mum looked at the iron in its stand, and back at the wrist, and didn't let go. Her thumb stayed against the inside of Amara's arm, just under the scald, where it wasn't sore. "You burned yourself on Wednesday, and walked about in drain water on Thursday with it open, and didn't say."

"It's fine. It doesn't hurt."

"It's weeping." Mum let go and got the tin down from above the fridge, and put a dressing on it, square and white, pressing the edges flat with her fingers one side at a time. Amara held still for it. Mum had her meeting face on, the calm one, and her hands were too careful.

"Tuesday you're coming with me," Mum said.

"To the canal rooms?"

"I'm there till ten at least. I'm not having you down at that lake in the dark with your arm like this and nobody knowing where you are. You can sit at the back. Bring a book. Bring the box, if you like. There's a whole canal you can point it at."

Tuesday was meant to be the house to herself till eleven and the culvert with nobody asking. Now it was a plastic chair at the back of a room in town, an hour away, watching Mum say I hear you to people.

"Okay."

"Is that a yes? I want a yes."

"Yes."

Mum nodded, once, the way she did when a thing went in the diary. She put the papers back under her arm and drank half her tea, and kissed the top of Amara's head going past, and the front door went, and then the car.

Amara sat with the dressing on her wrist and the box in front of her. The needle still rested a hair off zero, where the pin had bent. On her phone Mum's third text from yesterday was still unanswered, and under it the three from Hyejin, still unanswered too. She opened Isabel's instead.

I've fixed the meter. Can you come out on Sunday and watch me hold it to the grate? I'll tell you before I move.

Isabel's flat was cold when they got back to it, and Hoshi was at the corner behind the desk, yowling at the join of the two walls. When Isabel came in the cat stopped, and looked at her, and turned back to the plaster and started again.

Natalie went straight to the sink and ran the cold tap. "Hand," she said.

Isabel gave it to her. Natalie peeled the gauze back with her fingertips, a corner at a time where it had stuck. Under it the scald across her knuckles had opened along its middle when she made the fist, and the long one had wept into it where they crossed. Natalie held the whole back of the hand under the water.

It was Natalie's right hand doing the holding, palm up under Isabel's, and across the base of it, over the callus, there was a scald Isabel hadn't seen in the lane. Copper-coloured, a thumb wide, raw at the edges.

"What's that?"

"Grate in Salter's Lane. The frost had it down in the iron."

"Did you get it?"

"No. It'll keep till there's a thaw." Natalie turned Isabel's hand a little so the water ran over the knuckles. "Say the thaw comes Tuesday. Five in the morning, Salter's Lane. How do you come at it?"

"From the top, not the bottom, because the bottom's always got the bins." Isabel thought. "And it'll be in the bars, not the stone. So you feel the iron first."

"And after that?"

Natalie's left hand had gone into her coat pocket while she asked, and something in there crackled, folded paper, the same sound as yesterday on the way out the door.

It was nearly the game from when Isabel was new, five years of walking behind Natalie at dawn and being asked what came next. Only then Natalie had never asked how Isabel would come at a thing, or said a day. "The Tangle's wall. The stall gutter, if it's been raining. Then the towpath, the two past the lock, the chapel yard, which freezes first, and the long one at the tram stop, which you do from the kerb or you get your feet wet. Then home."

Natalie turned the hand under the tap. "You've got it all. The whole round." Her other hand came out of the pocket empty.

So Isabel had passed. Five years, and one root gone under a building, and she was back to being asked the round like it was her first winter. Her phone had gone off on the walk back. She fished it out of her jacket left-handed and read it out over the sink, so Natalie would hear it.

I've fixed the meter. Can you come out on Sunday and watch me hold it to the grate? I'll tell you before I move.

She put it face down on the bench. "Amara. Full stops and all. I told her that yesterday, at the culvert, you know? Tell me before you move. It's the one thing I said that she listened to."

Natalie shut the tap off and patted Isabel's hand dry with the tea towel, round the scalds, not on them. "She's saying it, then," she said. "Somebody ought to be there to hear it."

Somebody. Yesterday in her kitchen it had been her cut and her jar. Now she was being let go to Linden Rise, like a schoolkid going on an excursion.

"I wasn't asking." She took the hand back. The words had come out harder than she'd meant, and she didn't take them back either. "I went out there yesterday on my own. Nobody had to say I could."

Natalie got clean gauze out of the chemist's bag and held out her hand, and waited until Isabel gave hers back.

"Say it, then," Isabel said. "This morning. Whatever it is."

Natalie started winding, round the knuckles and across the back and round the wrist, not too tight. "You felt it going on you and you didn't call me off the stair," she said. "You kept the staff on the wall. That's the thing I'd want from anybody."

"That's what lost it."

"It went either way."

"You don't know that."

"No," Natalie said. She tied off the gauze and tucked the end under. "Where's the jar?"

"Jacket."

"Keep the lid on it. She'll want it clean when you bring it."

Isabel looked at Natalie's wet trouser leg. The heater worked if you kicked it, and an hour on it would dry a sock, at least. She didn't offer it.

Natalie filled the kettle and switched it on, and got a mug down and put a teabag in it, one mug, and left it by the kettle for Isabel. She did up her coat over the wet trouser leg and went, and her boot squelched on every step of the stairs down.

The kettle came to the boil and clicked off. Isabel poured it, one-handed, and stood at the bench with it going cold, and got her phone up with her left thumb.

sunday, 10. don't go near the grate till i'm there.

She sent it. Behind the desk, at the cold corner, Hoshi drew breath and started again.

entry.title: Ironwood · Day 2: The Culvert Grate Where Amara Walked Out Ahead of the Staff
entry.content:
Thursday 5 July 2046, morning

Lost a cat near the Linden Rise culvert, grey with one white ear. Please ring before it gets dark.Handwritten notice taped to a bus shelter, Linden Rise

Natalie walked Isabel home along the river, the long way, with the water brown and high against the wall and the sky the grey of an old dishcloth. On the second-floor landing of Isabel's walk-up in the north lanes, Isabel got her key into the door and heard Hoshi before it opened.

The yowl came from the corner behind the desk. It was the same one as last night, low and long with a hitch at the end, aimed at the join of two walls where there was nothing but plaster and a curl of old tape. When Isabel came in, Hoshi stopped and looked at her. Then she turned back to the corner and started again.

"She's been doing that all week," Isabel said. "Day and night. Same corner."

Natalie stood just inside the door with her hands in her coat pockets. She didn't take the coat off.

Isabel went round the desk and put her palm flat on the plaster where Hoshi was looking. It was colder than the rest of the wall. Hoshi wound once round her ankle and yowled at her knee.

She filled the bowl, which Hoshi ignored, and put the kettle on, for something to do with her hands. Behind her she could feel Natalie looking at her, with the same gaze with which she pinned a wall before she touched it.

She had worked out the sentence on the river path. Every blight that grew nerves went in Elspeth Hale's book on Garnet Street, with its ash in a jar, and for five years every jar of Isabel's had gone there in Natalie's hand. Just the night before last, Natalie hadn't taken her word that the root was dead, had checked it anyway. Every time Natalie took a thing off her she made it sound like a favour. If it was going to stop, it had to be said before Natalie could offer.

"I'm going to finish the north cut," she said to the kettle. "Tomorrow, probably. On my own."

"Okay."

That was too easy. Natalie said okay to things and then turned up anyway, at the end of the lane, with her hand out. Isabel got two mugs down. "And I'm taking the jar to Garnet Street. Myself."

Natalie looked at her. It went on a moment longer than a look needed to. Then she said, "What are you putting it in?"

"A jar?"

"Which jar."

Isabel opened the cupboard and held one up. "Pesto. It's finished."

"Wash it twice and get the label off. All of it, the glue too. She'll pick at it if you don't." Natalie took one hand out of her pocket and pointed. "And a lid that screws. Not one that clips."

"Is that a rule?"

"That's Elspeth."

The kettle clicked off. Isabel didn't pour. "So it's mine. The cut and the jar. You're not going to turn up at the end of the lane and hold your hand out."

"It's yours," Natalie said. "Both."

So there would be a step on Garnet Street, and her on it, and nobody in front of her to hand it to. Isabel poured, and slopped some, and wiped it with her sleeve.

The thing she wanted next she wasn't going to ask for. She talked about the trains instead. "It's the Kilbride line to Breen's Crossing, then a bus out to the ring road. I'll be back by four. Five, if the bus does the thing where it sits at the Centre for twenty minutes."

"Come and find me at the canal rooms when you're in," Natalie said. "Eight or so. The 14 stops outside."

"What's at the canal rooms?"

"Friends of the Tangle. I'm not going in."

"A night out. On a footpath, outside a residents' meeting."

"There's an urn in there. I'll nick you a tea."

"Stolen tea."

"Council tea. It's not stealing, it's rates." Natalie took the mug Isabel held out and drank half of it standing, too hot, the way she always did.

She put the mug down on the desk, by Hoshi, and went. Her hand was back in her coat pocket before the door shut, holding something in there that crackled like folded paper.

Isabel ran the hot tap over the pesto jar and started on the label with her thumbnail. Behind her, in the corner, Hoshi started again.

Isabel came off the bus at the ring road just after ten, an hour out from her own lanes, and felt the ground at Linden Rise come up through her boots wrong. At home her line ran under her like her own stair in the dark. Here the pull under her feet was thin and young, laid over ten years of identical roofs, and it belonged to somebody else. It was like walking through a stranger's house with the lights off.

The drain lake was still over the path at the culvert. Amara Nwosu was waiting on the bench by the water with a box on her knees and a can from the school's vending machine going cold beside her. She was fifteen and looked it: school jacket, hood up, a satchel strap across her chest.

"Hi. You came." Amara stood. "I fixed it. The meter. Last night, at the kitchen table. It was the ground wire, and a joint, I think, so I did both."

"Cool," Isabel said, and meant it, and didn't know what else to say about a box.

Then Amara called her staff, and it was in her hands, pale green wood that smelled of sap from where Isabel stood, and the rest of her went with it. She was taller than Isabel. She looked twenty-two, twenty-three. Copper ran down both her forearms into the wood, and she stood in the wet with her weight easy on both feet, as though nothing anywhere was hurrying her and nothing ever would.

Isabel called her own. The staff came pale into her palms, the copper warm along her arms, the shape settling on her. She waded out until the water was over her ankles and the static came in at the back of her head, loud, a bad line with somebody shouting on the other end of it. It came from behind the grate where the reeds had jammed.

"Okay," Isabel said. "Stay at the edge. Two things first."

Amara stayed at the edge. Isabel was grateful for that, for about a second.

"Nerves first. If it's grown nerves, you take those off before you go anywhere near the heart."

"Why?"

"So it can't feel you coming."

"What does it do if it feels you?"

"Runs."

"Runs where?"

Isabel opened her mouth and nothing was in it. Natalie had said so it can't run, and Isabel had never asked where to. "Away. Deeper. Second thing, you never walk up on one alone."

"How close counts as alone?"

"It just- you don't do it."

"Okay." Amara nodded, once, as if she'd filed it. "But you're here. So I'm not alone." She stepped down into the water with the box held out in front of her. "Can I hold it to the grate while you watch? It's one joint. It should hold."

"Wait. I haven't told you how it goes yet."

"You told me. Nerves first, don't go alone. You're watching." She was already three steps out.

Isabel could have caught her by the sleeve. She thought of Natalie's hand closing on the staff, the coat, the key, and her own hand stayed where it was. Grabbing was what you did when you'd run out of things to say. Ten minutes in, and Amara would know that about her.

The needle in the box lifted. Amara took another step and it climbed past the felt-tip marks, past the last one, and hard against the stop.

Behind the grate, Isabel could see it now. A grey-brown mass the size of a car tyre was wedged into the mouth of the pipe, with the reed roots grown into its underside. Along its top edge stood a dozen pale threads, each about as long as a finger. They had all turned toward Amara.

Then the needle dropped back to nothing. Amara shook the box, and it rattled, and when she tipped it to the light Isabel could see the needle lying loose at the bottom, off its pin altogether.

The threads drew in. The mass slid back from the grate, a hand's width and then an arm's length, into the dark under the ring road, and the static went down to a mutter in the back of Isabel's skull. Where the reeds had been grown into it, their roots tore and floated up black.

Amara stood at the grate with the box against her chest. "It went higher than last time," she said. "Before it went. You saw it go higher."

"I saw," Isabel said. The water was cold through her boots. The blight was further in now than her staff could reach from the grate.

Amara Nwosu stood at the culvert grate at Linden Rise with a dead box against her chest and her staff in her other hand, and the signal went behind her teeth like a held note. It hadn't gone. It had only gone back.

She had cut two on her own before this one, this winter, and told nobody, Isabel least of all. Neither of them had felt like this.

"They'll come back to the light, and take them as they come. Put that on the bench," Isabel said, waving her hand at the box. "Then come back and stand where I tell you."

Amara put it on the bench, upside down so the needle wouldn't fall out, and waded back. Isabel put her a body's length to the left of the grate, on the shallow side, and went in close herself, until her staff was through the bars into the dark of the pipe.

They waited. The water came to Amara's shins. Then the threads came back out of the dark, slowly, feeling along the pipe floor toward the light.

Isabel pinned the first one. Amara watched the copper run out of her arms along the pale wood and into it, and the thread go grey and still. That was nerves first. That was the rule.

Amara shifted her weight to her right foot, and the signal shifted with her.

She stood very still. The rest of the threads had turned, in the water, away from Isabel's staff and toward her. She moved her left foot a hand's width along the bank. The pressure behind her teeth slid that hand's width too. Isabel was right there with her staff in the pipe, nearer than Amara by a whole body, and they weren't looking at Isabel at all.

Nobody had said anything about that. Not Isabel, not the forums.

"They're following me," Amara said. "Not you."

Isabel's head came round. "That's not- they feel whoever's closest."

"You're closest."

Isabel didn't answer that. Her hands were shaking on the staff. Amara could see it from where she stood, the end of the wood ticking against the bars.

"Okay but what if I walk, along the bank, really slowly, and they come out after me, and you take them as they come? Is that a dumb idea? It might be a dumb idea."

"Natalie never said anything about doing it like that."

"Is it wrong, though?"

Isabel breathed out through her mouth. "Go slow."

Amara went slow. The threads came out of the pipe after her, one by one, into the grey light at the grate's edge, and Isabel took them one by one as they cleared the bars. Four. Seven. Ten. Her copper was the inside of a two-pence piece held to a lamp, and Amara felt her own arms warm in answer every time Isabel leaned.

The last one whipped. It came off the grate in a flick and went along the water to Amara's staff, and up it, and over her wrist. On its way back it went across the back of Isabel's hand where she gripped the bars.

It went grey under Isabel's staff a second later. The signal dropped to a single low note, far in under the road.

Amara looked at her wrist. A scald ran from the bone at the outside of it a thumb's length up her forearm, along her copper, thin and wet. Across Isabel's raw knuckles ran a shorter one, the same colour, already weeping.

"The heart's under the road," Isabel said. "I can't reach it from here, and I'm not going in there. Without the nerves it can't feel us. It'll keep."

Amara wanted to ask how long keep was, and didn't. Isabel waded out of the water, slowly, and looked at her, and not at her wrist.

"Where'd you learn to stand like that?"

Amara had excuses ready, three of them, and every one was for the start of a thing. It was too late for any of them now. She looked at the water. "I read a lot," she said. "On the forums." It came out small.

"You don't learn your feet off forum posts." Isabel looked at her a moment more. "You've stood at one of these before."

Amara didn't say yes. She didn't say no either, and Isabel nodded slowly. So, she knew. Not that there were two, not where, but she knew that she had done this before, and now every time Amara asked her something Isabel would be wondering what else she already knew.

"Next time, tell me before you move," Isabel said. "Not after. Before."

That was all. Not that was right. Amara nodded and let the staff go, and her shape went with it, and the cold came straight through her school jacket. She was looking up at Isabel now, not down.
