Isabel stayed as she was a while after, staff across her knees on the bench, copper still running faint down her arms. Then she let it go too.

"You're taller than me in it," Isabel said.

"I'm still growing, though," Amara said. "Out of it, I mean. I've gone through two pairs of school shoes this year. So I'll catch you up anyway."

Isabel said her bus went at the half hour.

Amara's phone went three times in her pocket. Mum texted in threes, and the third was always the question. Mum was at work till six.

Did you have lunch?

Chicken's defrosting in the sink, put it in the fridge by three please.

Where are you today?

Yes, I had a sandwich.

I'll do it now.

She left the third. Under it, further down the screen, sat three messages from a girl called Hyejin, who had written to her the night she posted: what it costs, how girls die, that nobody is coming. She had read them twice each. She hadn't answered those either.

She pulled her sleeve down over her wrist before Isabel could look at it.

Elspeth Hale opened the door of her house on Garnet Street before Natalie had knocked twice, and looked past her, down the step, to see who wasn't on it.

"Just me," Natalie said.

"So I see." Elspeth was in a cardigan nobody had made since Natalie was at school, and a skirt older than the cardigan. She looked seventeen. She had looked seventeen when Natalie first stood on this step, and when Natalie's mother was a girl. She stood back to let her in.

The front room was as it always was. The ledger lay open on the table, the last line in grey-brown ink: The Hundred and Third: Sagittaria. Beside it sat the ink stone, wiped and dry, and the steel nib on its rest, and a row of clean jars with nothing in them.

"I've had the stone out since Tuesday night," Elspeth said. "You posted it done."

"The nerves are done. The cut isn't. I should have written it that way."

"Then I've had the stone out two days for half a job."

"A bit longer, then. Iz is closing it tomorrow. She'll be bringing the jar."

Elspeth sat, and folded her hands on her knees. Natalie stayed standing. "Quiet girl. I don't think I've ever caught her eyes when she's stood behind you here."

"She's grown, over these years." Natalie put her hand in her coat pocket and kept it there, off the letter from Mum, folded in thirds. "It's time her name went in."

Elspeth looked at the empty jars. "And when she's brought it," she said, "and I've written her, who does she bring the next one to, after me?"

"Not me."

"You've a steady hand. You know every girl in the Bay by her walk."

"I said no at Easter. It's still no."

The words were said, and heard, and yet Natalie could tell the question would be back.

"Then I'll ask the girl who's been walking the edges of my parish for me. She seems willing."

There was the itch, faint, somewhere off toward Hollis Street. Nothing much. Not hers, either. Ward Seven had been Elspeth's as long as anyone could remember, and for a fortnight Natalie had been walking the far end of it on her way home, because it needed doing and wasn't being done. Natalie thought of the old core at dawn tomorrow, the grates and the lanes and the five-minute cuts, and of it some other morning with nobody on it at all, and only one somebody she could think of to put there.

"And your friend. How is she?"

Elspeth had called every one of them friend, the ones Natalie slept with and the ones she didn't, in the same voice. There was no telling from the word what she'd put in the book this time.

"Isabel's teaching. Out at Linden Rise."

"The new growth." Elspeth never learned the names out there. "There's a girl out there three weeks found who hasn't come to me."

"That's the one."

"Is that so?" Elspeth looked at her for a while, the long patient look she gave everything, as though it were a matter for the record. Then she got up, closed the ledger on its ribbon, and set the nib straight on its rest. "I'll hold the Hundred and Fourth. I'll not write it for anybody else, and I'll not take that jar from your hand. She knows the way?"

"I'll tell her."

At the door Elspeth said, "Mind the bridge on your way."

"I know," Natalie said, and went down the step with her hand still in her pocket.

Isabel came back into the north lanes late in the afternoon and went straight to Kell's Lane without going home first, because if she went home first she'd sit down.

The lane looked as it always did: stacked windows, the fire stair down one side, a pram somebody had left under it. The static was faint. She had to stand still in the middle of the cobbles for a full minute before she found it, a thin bad line behind her ear that kept dropping out. On Tuesday night she'd walked off this cut half done and the opening had been right there under her heel. It wasn't there now.

She called her staff. Her arms complained, after the culvert. She laid the pale wood along the cobbles where she'd left the seam and felt for it.

It had closed over. Not straight, the way she'd opened it, but crooked, knitting back on itself across the lane and then off sideways, under the fire stair, toward the foot of the block wall. She followed it with the staff end, a step at a time, losing it and finding it.

"You'll catch your death, down there on your knees."

Mrs Vella had come out onto her back step, which gave onto Kell's Lane, with a basket of washing on her hip. She'd been on Linnet Lane forty years and she knew who was in and who was out and who wasn't eating, and she treated all of it as her business.

"I'm good," Isabel said. "Dropped something."

"It's been cold in this lane since Tuesday night. Colder than the weather. I said so this morning to anyone who'd listen." Mrs Vella pegged out a pillowcase. "The little ones from number nine play down that end. Should I be keeping them off?"

Isabel didn't answer yet. She'd lost the seam at the bottom step of the fire stair. To find where it really went she had to push into it, and she knew that, and she did it: leaned, and let the copper run out along the staff into the knit.

The seam pushed back. It came up the staff the way the thread had come up Amara's that morning and went over the back of her hand, over the scald she already had from the culvert. When she looked, the new one ran from the second knuckle to the wrist bone, copper-coloured and wet, crossing the first.

She swore at it, quietly.

But she had it now. The true line went under the fire stair, along the foot of the wall for about four metres, and stopped at the downpipe. All of it would have to be opened again along its length and held while she went for the root. On Tuesday night it would have been ten minutes. Now it was an hour, maybe more, and all of it holding.

She could start now. It was light for another two hours. She had nothing left in her arms after the culvert, and she could feel the shape thin at her edges already, the way it went before it slipped. She held it anyway, a moment longer, crouched by the downpipe, before she let it go.

Tomorrow. After Natalie's round. She didn't look at why that was the time she'd picked.

"Keep them off the stair end," she said. "Just till tomorrow. The cobbles are lifting."

"The cobbles have been lifting since nineteen-ninety." Mrs Vella looked at her hand. Isabel put it in her pocket. "Come in and have a cup of tea. I've the kettle on and nobody to drink it."

"I've got to be somewhere at eight."

"It's half five."

"I've got to feed the cat."

"That cat," Mrs Vella said, "has been shouting at the wall since breakfast. I could hear it from the yard." She held the back door open with her hip and waited, with the empty basket, and did not go in.

Natalie was outside the community rooms by the canal when Iz came in on the 14, a little after eight. Behind the glass the Friends of the Tangle had the lights on and the stacking chairs out in rows, and somebody was standing at the front with a sheet of paper. Every pole on the street wore one of Hyejin Park's flyers, SAVE THE TANGLE over a hand-drawn vine, some of them three deep. Natalie had walked past twenty-one years of Hyejin and never once asked her anything. Down the line at the Exchange the Back Room was on, and she wasn't going to that either.

The canal was high from last night, black and quick against the brick. A little way along, past the lock, the patch by the bridge sat where it always sat, and pulled.

Iz came off the tram with her hand in her jacket pocket and her shoulders up round her ears. She hadn't slept much, and she'd used herself up somewhere today. Natalie didn't say so.

"No tea," Natalie said. "They've got a woman guarding the urn."

"Council security. Figures."

They stood under the pole. Iz told it in order, the way she told everything: the bus, the drain over the path, the girl on the bench, the box that went to the stop and then dropped its needle. The threads that turned. The girl walking the bank so they'd come out after her. The heart under the ring road. Natalie listened and looked at the water past the lock, and made herself look back.

"They followed her," Iz said. "Not me. I was closer. You never said anything about that."

"No."

"Is that a thing?"

"Not one I've seen." Which was true, and narrower than the question.

"And Kell's Lane's knitted over crooked. It goes under the fire stair and along the wall to the downpipe. It's an hour now, holding the whole way." Iz stopped. Her eyes had gone past Natalie's shoulder, toward the bridge, and come back. "You keep looking at the bridge."

"Water's up."

Iz waited, and when nothing else came she let it go, and Natalie watched her decide to.

"So tomorrow," Iz said. "After your round. I want you there. Watching. Not doing anything. Just there."

The itch was faint and far off and nothing to do with this. Natalie thought of a wall four metres long and Iz holding it open alone with nothing in her arms, and threads that went for the wrong girl.

"I'll come straight to Kell's Lane from the round," she said. "Seven, about."

"And watch."

"Iz. Look at your hand."

Iz looked at her hand under the streetlight. There were two scalds across the back of it, crossing, both weeping. She stuffed it back in her pocket. "You said it was mine. This morning, you said both."

"The jar's yours. I've told Elspeth. She won't take it off me if I turn up with it. She'll hold it for you."

"That's not what I asked."

"I know. I'll take the stair end. You do the rest."

"So you'll watch me do three metres of it and then you'll do the bit that's hard."

"I'll do the bit where you can't see the root." Natalie could hear herself, and couldn't make herself say the other thing.

Isabel's shoulders came down, not the way they had this morning in the kitchen, and she looked off to the side, not meeting Natalie's eyes anymore. "Seven, then."

"Seven."

The door of the rooms banged open behind them, and a man in a fleece came out with a roll of tape and a fresh stack of flyers. He taped one to the pole beside Natalie's head, over the old ones, and smoothed the vine flat with his thumb. The 14 came back round the other way, and Iz got on it without looking back. Natalie walked home by Weir Street, not the towpath, past a flyer on every pole.

entry.title: Ironwood · Day 1: The Answer Given in Daylight on the Canal Bank
entry.content:
Wednesday 4 July 2046, morning

DO NOT USE THE TOWPATH AFTER HEAVY RAIN.Council notice, cable-tied to the railing of the old canal bridge

Amara Nwosu stood ankle-deep where the night's rain had pushed the drain lake over the path, at the culvert under the ring road at Linden Rise. Water still ran off the concrete above her in cold strings. The reeds along the lake had jammed against the grate in the night, and where they met the water they had gone black at the root.

The signal sat behind her teeth and at the back of her head. That was how the blight felt to her: a pressure that got stronger the closer she came. It was strong now.

In both hands she held the meter, a box of her own wiring, the dial marked in felt-tip at midnight and the needle loose on its pin. It was meant to read what her head read. She had run out of time before the ground wire, and one end hung bare inside.

She wanted to see it work. She wanted to show it to Isabel, the girl who had replied to her post. Isabel would be impressed, right? And then she'd be able to learn how to cut cleanly, and what worked and what didn't, and she'd be good at it. Especially with this blight, whose pressure was nothing like the two she'd cut before. Sharper, like a migraine. She moved, and she almost felt something move with her. Was it watching her?

She turned toward the grate. The needle stirred, twitching. Did that count? She held the box out at arm's length, stretching, trying to be close to and far from the grate at the same time. The needle lifted, climbed, and then dropped completely. As she pulled it back, it stayed dead.

She shook the box. Nothing, just a slight rattle. She didn't have her screwdriver here, but she could already tell it was wire banging around. Probably a cold solder joint.

So the box worked, or near enough. She felt her grin coming through, and tamped it down. Be professional.

She checked her phone again. No response from Isabel. She waited, tapping her foot, and then the drizzle found the gap at her collar and she checked again.

She could go nearer, and find out what this blight did with someone standing that close to it. Or she could stay where she was, in water to the ankle, and wait for the girl who wasn't there, and might not show up at all. The forums said a girl didn't walk up on one that might have nerves, not alone.

She stayed. The cold came through her boots and into her toes. She counted to ten between checks, caught herself at it, and made a face. God, she was such a kid.

Still, nothing. She waited.

Isabel woke in Natalie's flat, expecting to find a weight behind her back and feeling nothing instead. The sheet on Natalie's side was cold, and when Isabel got up, she noticed the coat gone from its hook by the door. The mugs from last night were up on the bench, beside the sink. The keys weren't in the dish. Natalie had them, then. Probably.

She stood and looked at the couch for a moment too long. Last night Natalie had told her about the ditch under the old canal bridge, and stopped halfway through, and Isabel did not have to think about where to look. She dressed quickly, grabbed her phone, and left the flat.

She went out along the towpath, the damp of yesterday's jacket chilling her. The canal had come over the path in places and the mud squelched around her boots. The old bridge came up out of the drizzle, and below it, halfway down the bank on the wet grass, Natalie was going carefully toward the black water. She hadn't looked up yet.

Isabel stood for a moment, weighing. If she stayed here, Natalie would keep going. If she called out, Natalie might stop. But then they'd have to talk.

"Natalie."

Natalie stopped. For a moment she stood as she was, one foot lower than the other on the slope. Then she turned and came back up, and stood on the path next to Isabel, close but not.

Isabel made herself look at her face. "What are you doing out here?"

Natalie turned and looked back at the flood-swelled canal running past. Water ran off her hair and down her jaw, and she didn't wipe it. There was something in the way her eyes stared, Isabel thought, but she couldn't describe it. As the moment stretched, she gave it up. "You don't have to tell me. Sorry."

"It's okay. It's not something I'm ready to talk about just yet. You'll have to be patient with me on that. Okay?"

"Okay." A beat, and her stomach grumbled, which set off a small giggle from Natalie, and then the two were laughing, breath fogging in the air.

"Come on, let's go back to mine," Natalie said. "I'll do eggs. Proper ones."

They went up past the bridge, where a council notice had been cable-tied to the railing, laminated, gone cloudy with rain. DO NOT USE THE TOWPATH AFTER HEAVY RAIN. Natalie read it out, flat as a newsreader, and looked down at the water over both their boots.

"Bit late," Isabel said, with a smile. "Did you take the keys? I didn't lock up. I couldn't find them."

Natalie patted her coat pocket, and it jangled. "Always."

"Okay. Good." Isabel looked ahead along the towpath, where it went under again past the lock. "We should cut up by the garages. It'll be drier."

"You've thought about this."

"I try," Isabel demurred. Natalie made a small sound that might have been a laugh, and let her lead.

It was always easier to talk to Natalie, and she wanted to figure out why, but maybe not this morning. Not after how hard it had been last night. This morning, she would just enjoy it. Or try to.

She felt a buzz in her pocket, the girl from the forums. Right. She tapped out a quick reply, tossed the phone back in her pocket, and looked up as Natalie asked "Who's that?"

"The girl from the forums. She wants me to teach her."

Natalie didn't say anything for a few steps. "You going to?"

"Someone has to." Left unsaid was whether she could. Isabel knew she could. It didn't need saying.

The silence grew legs and shadowed them. As they stopped at the next traffic light, something simmered in her, and a question burst out.

"I need to know. Was last night real? To you?"

A breath, and then another. "It's real," Natalie said.

Isabel shifted, her hands unclenched. Then she looked for the rest of it in Natalie's face, the catch or the lie or anything at all, and found the calm Natalie wore on a cut, and nothing past it.

Then why leave? Why the bridge? Next time she would be up before the coat left the hook.

At the grate, Amara went to message Isabel again.

Can you show me how to cut today? I've done two already, but this one's different.

She backspaced the second part out, and tapped send. If Isabel knew, she might say no, she might think Amara was getting ahead of herself.

This time the answer came inside a minute.

sure

tomorrow? after 10

Amara replied with a time and place before she could think, and retreated to a bench, phone in her pocket. It was damp, and she sat anyway. Not like she was getting any drier today.

She pulled out the box again, turned it over in her hands. She had been excited to show it to Isabel; barely started and already she was doing things that no one else had done. But now she had no proof. She tossed it back in her satchel.

She ran through the questions she wanted to ask. She wanted to be sophisticated, didn't want to be asking beginner questions. "How often do you walk your rounds?" she asked the air. Or, perhaps, one from the forum, "How long do you give a root before you call it dead?" No one was around to hear her pondering, it was a miserable day to be outside. "How close can you get before it notices you?" Nah, too basic.

A yawn forced its way out of her tight jaw, and Amara remembered that vending machine outside the school. She meandered over and grabbed a can of hot coffee, making a noise at the bitter taste. At least it was something warm to hold, and eventually she'd get used to it, she supposed.

She wandered back to the bench to wait, hands warm and eyes open.
